title: health-food
text: This project investigates physical measurements and health metrics from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), provided by the primer.data R package.

title: health-food
section: Food Consumption Trends: Ultra-Processed vs. Minimally Processed Foods
text:
Food Consumption Trends: Ultra-Processed vs. Minimally Processed Foods
This graph tracks the proportion of daily calories coming from ultra-processed foods (shown in red) compared to whole and minimally processed foods (shown in green) among US adults over time.










Opposing Trends: As ultra-processed foods rose from 52.5% in 1999–2000 to over 57% by 2018–2020, whole and minimally processed foods fell from 33.5% to 27.4%.
Recent Shift: In the August 2021–August 2023 survey cycle, ultra-processed food intake dropped to 53.0%, while whole and minimally processed calories rose back to approximately 30.5%.

title: NHANES Health Insights
text:
The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) assesses the health and nutritional status of adults and children across the United States.

BMI TrajectoryObesity by AgeObesity Rates Over TimeHeart DiseaseUltra-Processed DietDiet-Related Diseases












Key Observations

Childhood to Early Adulthood: BMI increases sharply from childhood into the twenties as individuals grow.
Middle Adulthood: BMI levels tend to plateau between ages 30 and 60, with the average hovering in the 28–30 kg/m² range.
Later Decades: The trend line stabilizes and gently tapers downward in older age, following comparable paths for both males and females.















Beyond individual age trajectories, national health surveys track how adult obesity prevalence has shifted across recent decades.










Rising Trend: Between 1999–2000 and 2017–2018, the US adult obesity rate increased from 30.5% to over 42%.
Recent Leveling: Rates remained above 41% entering 2020, and the August 2021–August 2023 survey recorded 40.3%, pointing to a recent stabilization.











Individual Participant Points: Each dot represents an adult survey participant from that cycle (sampled at 120 participants per cycle). Green dots show individuals who are not obese (BMI < 30), and red dots show individuals who are obese (BMI ≥ 30).
Average Weight Trend Line: The solid black line tracks the average adult weight across each year, rising from approximately 174 lbs in 2000 to over 183 lbs in 2018–2020 as obesity rates climbed.
Trend Over Time (1999–2023): As the national adult obesity rate increased from 30.5% in 1999–2000 to over 42% in recent survey cycles, the proportion of red dots visibly rises across the timeline.



Heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States. This graph tracks the prevalence of diagnosed heart disease among US adults from 1999 to 2023.










Prevalence Stability: Approximately 11% of US adults live with diagnosed heart disease, holding relatively steady between 10.6% and 11.9% from 1999 through 2023.
Cardiovascular Health Impact: While medical innovations and medications have improved management, heart disease remains the #1 cause of death in the US, strongly influenced by long-term metabolic health and obesity.



This graph tracks the proportion of daily calories coming from ultra-processed foods (shown in red) compared to whole and minimally processed foods (shown in green) among US adults over time.










Opposing Trends: As ultra-processed foods rose from 52.5% in 1999–2000 to over 57% by 2018–2020, whole and minimally processed foods fell from 33.5% to 27.4%.
Recent Shift: In the August 2021–August 2023 survey cycle, ultra-processed food intake dropped to 53.0%, while whole and minimally processed calories rose back to approximately 30.5%.



Poor diets high in ultra-processed foods, added sugars, sodium, and saturated fats contribute to several chronic health conditions. This chart tracks major diet-related conditions among US adults from 2000 to 2023.










Sharp Rise in Diabetes: Type 2 diabetes prevalence nearly doubled from 6.2% in 2000 to 11.6% in 2023, reflecting long-term increases in metabolic risk factors.
Cardiometabolic Clustering: Hypertension (high blood pressure) and obesity remain the most widespread conditions, consistently affecting more than one-third of American adults.
